items.stem: The Karlin–Rubin theorem guarantees a UMP test when the alternative is:
options: one-sided and the family has MLR
items.explanation: The Karlin–Rubin theorem gives a UMP test for a one-sided alternative when the family has a monotone likelihood ratio in a suitable statistic.

items.stem: The two-sided (1 − α) confidence interval for μ with σ unknown is:
items.explanation: With unknown population variance and a normal sample, (X̄−μ)/(S/√n) follows t with n−1 degrees of freedom. A two-sided interval uses the upper-tail t quantile at α/2.

items.stem: The (1 − α) lower confidence bound for μ with σ unknown is:
items.explanation: A lower one-sided confidence bound is X̄−tₙ₋₁,α S/√n. The corresponding confidence set extends from that lower endpoint to infinity.

items.stem: The pivot used for a confidence interval for σ² in a normal sample is:
items.explanation: distributed as χ² on n − 1 df

items.stem: Compared with a two-sided interval at the same confidence level, the one-sided bound uses:
items.explanation: A one-sided bound allocates all α to one tail and uses tₙ₋₁,α. A two-sided interval uses tₙ₋₁,α/2, which is larger; therefore the one-sided bound uses a smaller critical value.

items.stem: The degrees of freedom of the t-pivot for μ are:
items.explanation: One df is spent estimating μ by X̄ inside S

items.stem: To halve the width of a confidence interval for μ, the sample size must be multiplied by:
items.explanation: The interval width is proportional to 1/√n when confidence level and variability are fixed. To halve the width, √n must double, so n must be multiplied by 4.

items.stem: A pivotal quantity is one whose:
options: distribution is free of unknown parameters
items.explanation: A pivotal quantity has a sampling distribution that does not depend on unknown model parameters. This parameter-free distribution is what permits confidence limits to be constructed.

items.stem: If σ is known, the (1 − α) upper confidence bound for μ is:
items.explanation: When σ is known, (X̄−μ)/(σ/√n) is standard normal. The upper one-sided confidence bound is X̄+zα σ/√n, giving the interval (−∞, upper bound).

items.stem: “A 95% confidence interval for μ” correctly means:
options: 95% of such intervals in repeated sampling contain μ
95% of the data lie in the interval
the sample mean is within the interval 95% of the time
μ lies in this particular interval with probability 0.95
items.explanation: A 95% confidence procedure has 95% long-run coverage: over repeated samples, 95% of intervals constructed by the procedure contain the fixed parameter μ.

items.stem: As the confidence level rises from 90% to 99%, the interval:
items.explanation: A larger quantile is needed. items.stem: For a one-parameter exponential family and H₁: θ ≠ θ₀, a UMP test:
items.explanation: For a two-sided alternative, the most powerful rejection region generally depends on which side of the null is true. A single uniformly most powerful test therefore generally does not exist.

items.stem: The Neyman–Pearson lemma applies to:
items.explanation: The Neyman–Pearson lemma identifies the most powerful size-α test for a simple null hypothesis against a simple alternative hypothesis.

items.stem: For H₀: θ = θ₀ vs H₁: θ > θ₀ in exponential(θ), the UMP test rejects for:
items.explanation: A larger θ means a smaller mean 1/ θ, so small ΣXᵢ is evidence for H₁

items.stem: The likelihood ratio test statistic λ satisfies:
items.explanation: It is a supremum over a subset divided by a supremum over the whole space

items.stem: Asymptotically, −2 log λ follows:
options: χ² with df equal to the number of restrictions
items.explanation: Wilks' theorem states that under regularity conditions, −2 log λ converges in distribution to a chi-square variable whose degrees of freedom equal the number of independent restrictions imposed by H₀.

items.stem: For H₀: θ = θ₀ vs H₁: θ ≠ θ₀ in N(μ, σ²) with σ² known, the two-sided z test is:
items.explanation: Same principle: two-sided alternatives give UMPU, not UMP

items.stem: The likelihood ratio statistic λ satisfies:
items.explanation: The null parameter space is contained in the full parameter space. Maximising over the larger space cannot give a smaller likelihood, so the likelihood ratio is between zero and one.

items.stem: The LR test rejects H₀ when:
items.explanation: A small likelihood ratio means the best fit under H₀ is much worse than the unrestricted best fit. The LR test therefore rejects for sufficiently small λ (equivalently, large −2 log λ).

items.stem: The LR test statistic depends on the data through:
items.explanation: For a regular exponential-family model, the likelihood can be expressed through its sufficient statistic. The likelihood ratio therefore depends on the sample through that statistic.

items.stem: For testing H₀: μ = μ₀ in N(μ, σ²) with σ² unknown, the LR test is equivalent to:
items.explanation: For a normal sample with unknown variance, testing a specified mean by the likelihood ratio leads to the same rejection rule as the usual two-sided Student t test.

items.stem: If H₀ imposes 3 independent restrictions, the asymptotic df of −2 log λ is:
items.explanation: Wilks' chi-square approximation uses one degree of freedom for each independent restriction under the null. Three independent restrictions therefore give 3 degrees of freedom.

items.stem: For a simple null against a simple alternative, the LR test:
items.explanation: For a simple null against a simple alternative, the likelihood-ratio ordering gives the Neyman–Pearson most powerful test at the chosen size.

items.stem: λ = 1 indicates:
options: the maximum over Θ₀ equals the maximum over Θ, so H₀ fits as well as possible
items.explanation: If λ=1, the maximum likelihood under the null equals the unrestricted maximum. The null model fits as well as the full model for the observed sample.

items.stem: The LR test is invariant under:
items.explanation: A one-to-one reparameterisation preserves the likelihood ordering and therefore leaves the likelihood-ratio test unchanged.

items.stem: For testing H₀: σ² = σ₀² in a normal sample, the LR test leads to a critical region based on:
items.explanation: Under a normal sample with the mean estimated, (n−1)S²/σ₀² has a chi-square distribution with n−1 degrees of freedom under H₀. The LR critical region is based on this variance statistic.

items.stem: The power of a test equals:
items.explanation: Power is the probability of rejecting H₀ when H₁ is true. Since β is the probability of a Type II error, power=1−β.

items.stem: A Type I error occurs when:
items.explanation: A Type I error occurs when the test rejects H₀ even though H₀ is true.

items.stem: For f(x) = 1/θ on [0, θ], testing H₀: θ = 1 vs H₁: θ = 3 with critical region x ≥ 0.6, the power is:
items.explanation: Under θ=3, X is uniform on [0,3]. The probability of falling in the rejection region [0.6,3] is (3−0.6)/3=0.8.

items.stem: For X~Uniform(0,θ), testing H₀:θ=1 against H₁:θ>1 by rejecting when X≥0.6, the size is:
items.explanation: Under H₀:θ=1, X is uniform on [0,1]. The size is P(X≥0.6|θ=1)=(1−0.6)/1=0.4.

items.stem: For fixed sample size, decreasing α causes β to:
items.explanation: For a fixed sample size, making the rejection region smaller to reduce α generally makes it harder to reject under alternatives too, so β increases.

items.stem: A test is unbiased if:
options: it uses an unbiased es timator
items.explanation: A test is unbiased when its power under every parameter value in the alternative is at least its size α.

items.stem: A test is consistent if, as n → ∞, the power tends to:
items.explanation: A test is consistent if its power tends to one as the sample size increases for every fixed alternative in the relevant parameter space.

items.stem: The power of a test generally increases when:
options: the alternative moves closer to the null
items.explanation: Increasing sample size generally makes fixed departures from the null easier to detect, so the power increases when the test size and alternative are held fixed.

items.stem: The first step in testing a hypothesis is:
items.explanation: Hypothesis testing begins by stating the null and alternative hypotheses. The test statistic and rejection rule are chosen only after the hypotheses are specified.

items.stem: The null hypothesis always contains:
items.explanation: The null hypothesis is conventionally formulated with an equality component, such as μ=μ₀ or p≤p₀ with the boundary equality used to calibrate the test.

items.stem: The p-value is:
options: P(data at least as extreme | H₀ true)
items.explanation: The p-value is calculated under H₀: it is the probability, assuming H₀, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one in the direction(s) specified by H₁.

items.stem: At significance level α, a null hypothesis is rejected when:
items.explanation: At significance level α, reject H₀ when the p-value is smaller than α. Otherwise, do not reject H₀.

items.stem: The significance level should be fixed:
options: before collecting or examining the data
items.explanation: Choose α before examining the data. Fixing the significance level in advance prevents the decision threshold from being selected to suit the observed result.

items.stem: “Failing to reject H₀” means:
options: there is insufficient evidence against H₀
items.explanation: Step 2 — conditional mean

items.stem: A result can be statistically significant but practically unimportant when:
items.explanation: With a very large sample, even a tiny effect can produce a small p-value. Statistical significance therefore does not necessarily imply practical importance.

items.stem: Performing many tests each at α = 0.05 causes:
options: the power to fall to zero
the overall type I error rate to rise
items.explanation: When many hypotheses are tested, the chance of at least one false rejection increases unless the procedure adjusts for multiplicity.

items.stem: The critical region is determined by:
options: α and the null distribution of the statistic
items.explanation: The critical region is selected so that its probability under the null distribution is α. Its location and shape therefore depend on α and the null distribution of the statistic.

items.stem: Choosing between a one-tailed and a two-tailed test should be based on:
options: the observed direction in the data
the alternative hypothesis stated in advance
items.explanation: The choice of a one-sided or two-sided alternative must be based on the scientific question and specified before observing the data, not selected after seeing the sample direction.

items.stem: The power of a test is:
items.explanation: Power is P(reject H₀|H₁ is true). It measures the probability that the test detects a specified alternative.

items.stem: If the power of a test is 0.72, then β equals:
items.explanation: The Type II error probability is the complement of power. Thus β=1−0.72=0.28.

items.stem: In a discrete test, an exact size of 0.05 is:
items.explanation: For discrete test statistics, the attainable rejection probabilities occur in jumps. A requested exact size may not be attainable without randomisation at the boundary.

items.stem: A randomised test is used to:
items.explanation: Randomisation at a boundary point allows a discrete test to attain a prescribed size exactly when a non-randomised rejection region can only undershoot it.

items.stem: For H₀: p = 0.5 vs H₁: p = 0.8 with n = 4 and critical region X = 4, the size is:
items.explanation: Under H₀, X~Binomial(4,0.5). For the critical region X=4, the size is P(X=4)=(0.5)⁴=1/16.

items.stem: For H₀:p=0.5 against H₁:p=0.8 with n=4, if the rejection region is X=4, the power is:
items.explanation: Under H₁, X~Binomial(4,0.8). For the critical region X=4, the power is P(X=4)=(0.8)⁴=0.4096.

items.stem: The binomial coefficients for n = 5 are:
items.explanation: The binomial coefficients for n=5 are the entries in row 5 of Pascal's triangle: 1, 5, 10, 10, 5, 1.

items.stem: If a test has size 0.5 and power 0.5, the test is:
items.explanation: Rejection is equally likely whether H₀ is true or false

items.stem: Tossing a fair coin 5 times and rejecting H₀: p = 1/2 when more than 3 heads occur gives a size of:
items.explanation: Under H₀, X~Binomial(5,1/2). Rejecting when more than three heads occur means X≥4, so the size is [C(5,4)+C(5,5)]/2⁵=6/32=3/16.

items.stem: In question 8, the power against p = 3/4 is:
items.explanation: Under p=3/4, the power for the same critical region X≥4 is C(5,4)(3/4)⁴(1/4)+(3/4)⁵=405/1024+243/1024=648/1024=81/128.

items.stem: For a one-parameter exponential family with a monotone likelihood ratio, a UMP test is generally available for which alternative?
options: A one-sided alternative in the appropriate direction
items.explanation: The monotone likelihood ratio property supports a UMP test for a one-sided alternative in the corresponding direction. A single UMP test generally does not exist for a two-sided alternative.

items.stem: The likelihood ratio statistic is defined as the supremum of the likelihood under the null divided by the supremum under:
items.explanation: The denominator maximises the likelihood over the full parameter space, which contains the null parameter space. Consequently the likelihood ratio lies between zero and one.

items.topic: Power of tests for a uniform model
items.stem: Let X have density 1/θ on 0 ≤ x ≤ θ. A test rejects H₀: θ=1 when X≥0.25. What is its power at θ=2?
items.explanation: Under θ=2, X is uniform on [0,2]. Thus Pθ=2(X≥0.25)=(2−0.25)/2=0.875.

items.topic: Power of tests for a uniform model
items.stem: For X ~ Uniform(0,θ), a test rejects when X≥c, where 0<c<1. Its size under H₀: θ=1 is:
items.explanation: Under the null, X is uniform on [0,1]. Therefore the rejection probability is P(X≥c)=1−c, which is the size.

items.stem: For a sample x₁,…,xₙ from an exponential distribution with rate λ, the maximum likelihood estimator of λ is:
items.explanation: The log-likelihood is n log λ−λΣxᵢ. Setting its derivative n/λ−Σxᵢ to zero gives λ̂=n/Σxᵢ=1/x̄.

items.stem: For n>1 observations from an exponential distribution with rate λ, the UMVUE of λ is:
items.explanation: The sum S=ΣXᵢ is complete sufficient and has Gamma(n, rate λ) distribution. Since E[(n−1)/S]=λ, this function of S is the UMVUE by Lehmann–Scheffé.

items.stem: If X₁,…,Xₙ are iid exponential(rate λ), then S=ΣXᵢ has which distribution?
items.explanation: A sum of n independent exponential variables with common rate λ has a Gamma distribution with shape n and rate λ.

items.stem: For S=ΣXᵢ from an iid exponential(rate λ) sample of size n, the pivot 2λS follows:
items.explanation: Since 2λXᵢ is χ²₂ for each exponential observation, summing n independent terms gives χ² with 2n degrees of freedom.

items.stem: The complete sufficient statistic for the rate λ in an iid exponential sample is:
items.explanation: The joint density factors through S=ΣXᵢ, making S sufficient. Its Gamma(n, rate λ) family is complete, so S is complete sufficient.

items.stem: For an exponential distribution parameterised by its mean θ, the maximum likelihood estimator of θ is:
items.explanation: The rate MLE is 1/x̄. Since θ=1/λ, invariance of maximum likelihood gives θ̂=x̄.

items.stem: For an iid exponential sample with mean θ, the sample mean X̄ is:
options: Always equal to the sample maximum
items.explanation: Each observation has expectation θ, so E(X̄)=n⁻¹ΣE(Xᵢ)=θ. Thus X̄ is unbiased for the population mean.

items.stem: For an iid exponential sample with mean θ and size n, Var(X̄) equals:
items.explanation: An exponential variable with mean θ has variance θ². Independence gives Var(X̄)=Var(X)/n=θ²/n.

items.stem: For X~Exponential(rate λ), the memoryless property is:
items.explanation: The survival function is e^(−λx). The conditional survival probability is e^(−λ(s+t))/e^(−λs)=e^(−λt)=P(X>t).

items.stem: If n=5 and the observed exponential sample sum is 10, the MLE of the rate λ is:
items.explanation: The exponential rate MLE is n/Σxᵢ. With n=5 and Σxᵢ=10, λ̂=5/10=0.5.
